standard_text: The kinetic theory of gases; the ideal gas; Boyle's law, Charles's law and the pressure–temperature law; the general gas equation p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂; the ideal gas equation pV = nRT; temperature in kelvin. key_sub: Always use the temperature in kelvin: T = θ + 273.
body_html:
How to think about it

The kinetic theory: a gas is made of particles in random motion; pressure is caused by collisions with the container walls; the average kinetic energy is proportional to the kelvin temperature. An ideal gas has particles with no volume and no forces between them.

Boyle's law: pV is constant at constant temperature. Charles's law: V/T is constant at constant pressure. For a fixed mass of gas p₁V₁/T₁ = p₂V₂/T₂. The ideal gas equation is pV = nRT, with R = 8,31 J·K⁻¹·mol⁻¹, p in Pa and V in m³.

Example

A gas at 300 K and 2 dm³ is heated to 600 K at constant pressure. New volume?

V/T is constant

Answer: 4 dm³

Example

Convert 27 °C to kelvin.

+273

Answer: 300 K

Common mistakes

  • Using °C in gas law calculations.
  • Using dm³ in pV = nRT without changing to m³.
  • Thinking gas particles stop at 0 °C.

faq.q: When do real gases behave least like ideal gases?
faq.a: At high pressure and low temperature, when the particles are close together and attract each other.

faq.q: Why does a tyre's pressure increase on a hot day?
faq.a: The particles move faster and hit the walls more often and harder.

items.q: Calculate the mean kinetic energy of a gas molecule at 273 K.
The plunger of a sealed syringe of air is pulled out slowly (constant temperature). What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles are spread over a larger volume, so they hit the walls less often.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “The forces of attraction between particles are strongest.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: Calculate the root-mean-square speed of carbon dioxide molecules (molar mass 0,0440 kg/mol) at 500 K.
What happens to the particles of a gas when its temperature rises?
c: They move faster: their average kinetic energy increases.
items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.e: The kinetic particle model: all matter is made of tiny particles in constant random motion.

items.q: How many degrees of freedom does a rigid non-linear polyatomic gas such as methane have at ordinary temperatures?
items.e: Translational and rotational motions each count.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “Particles slide past one another.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: A bicycle pump's outlet is blocked and the piston is pushed in slowly (constant temperature). Why does the pressure increase?
c: The same particles are in a smaller volume, so they hit the walls more often.
The mass of each particle changes.
The particles hit each other more often, not the walls.
items.e: Gas pressure comes from particles colliding with the walls of the container.

items.q: Which state of matter is described? “It can be compressed easily because there is a lot of space between particles.”
items.e: Solid: close, regular, vibrate. Liquid: close, random, slide past each other. Gas: far apart, random, fast.

items.q: A sealed syringe of air is put in a fridge. What happens to the pressure of the gas?
items.e: The particles move more slowly, so they hit the walls less often and with less force.
